mappings.note: Equal chords AB and CD with perpendiculars OP and OQ from the centre: the item runs on equal chords being equidistant from the centre and on OP bisecting AB. C-4.3-LO-4's third clause; LO-3 would be the code if central ANGLES were the subject.
The perpendicular from the centre bisects AB, giving a right triangle with hypotenuse 17 and one leg 15. C-4.3-LO-4 plus Pythagoras; the diameter is only there to supply the radius.
OD is perpendicular to AB, so it bisects it; the distance OC is found from 5 and 4, and CD is the remainder of the radius. All of it rests on C-4.3-LO-4's bisection property.

The right angle at B forces AC to be a diameter, which is the converse of LO-5's angle-in-a-semicircle result; the radius is then half AC, i.e. the circumcircle of the right triangle (LO-2's circumcentre clause).
Congruence of circles reduces to equal radii, because a circle is determined by its centre and radius alone. C-4.3-LO-1's definitional content.

If both diagonals are diameters, every vertex angle stands in a semicircle and is therefore a right angle (LO-5), so the cyclic quadrilateral is a rectangle (LO-6). Both steps are needed to rule out the parallelogram distractor.
OP > r places P outside, which follows directly from the circle being the locus of points at distance exactly r. C-4.3-LO-1's definition of a circle.
Exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points -- C-4.3-LO-2 verbatim, with 'infinite' as the distractor that belongs to the two-point case.

The chord nearer the centre is the longer one, which follows from the right triangle formed by the distance, half the chord and the radius. That relation is C-4.3-LO-4's equidistance clause; the item's 'symmetry' concept tag does not match it.

Competency: doubling the radius doubles the circumference. None of the six outcomes covers circumference or area -- they are all chord, angle and construction results -- so C-4.3's 'area in terms of pi' clause is the closest honest level.
The line of centres is the perpendicular bisector of the common chord, which is exactly the pair of results in C-4.3-LO-4 applied to both circles at once.
Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, so 70 degrees carries straight over. C-4.3-LO-3; LO-4 would be the code if a distance from the centre were involved.

Competency: a relation between a circle's radius and a square's side, which no chord or angle outcome covers. Cited at competency level also because the stem and the keyed answer disagree about which relation is wanted (see the defect list).
Three chords equidistant from the centre must be equal in length -- the converse direction of C-4.3-LO-4's 'equal chords are equidistant from the centre'.
The assertion about all diameters being equal is true; the reason inverts the radius-diameter relation and is false. Both statements are C-4.3-LO-1 definitional facts.
A square is cyclic because its opposite angles sum to 180 degrees -- the converse of C-4.3-LO-6's supplementary-angles theorem, which is what makes the reason explain the assertion.
Among the infinitely many circles through two points, the smallest has AB as diameter. That family of circles and its parametrisation by the perpendicular bisector is C-4.3-LO-2's first clause.
The SSS proof that equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre. C-4.3-LO-3's 'proves that' clause, in its forward direction.
Solves for x from the supplementary opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. C-4.3-LO-6, applied numerically.
Half the chord is 8, the distance is 6, so the radius is 10. C-4.3-LO-4's bisection property used with Pythagoras.
Equal inclination to the diameter makes the perpendiculars from the centre equal, and chords equidistant from the centre are equal. C-4.3-LO-4's equidistance clause, used in the converse direction.
The centre is equidistant from the chord's endpoints, so it lies on the chord's perpendicular bisector. The same family of chord-and-centre results as C-4.3-LO-4, stated as a locus argument.
Two opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral set equal to 180 degrees, solved for x and then for both angles. C-4.3-LO-6.

Computes a chord from its central angle: the 60 degree angle with two radii makes triangle OAB equilateral. The chord-to-central-angle correspondence is C-4.3-LO-3's territory; no distance from the centre is used, so not LO-4.
Derives chord = 2 root(r squared minus d squared) from the bisection property and Pythagoras. C-4.3-LO-4, asked as an explanation rather than a computation.

Equal chords AB and AC make triangles OAB and OAC congruent by SSS, so AO bisects the angle. The congruence is the same construction LO-3 uses, and the conclusion is about equal chords and the centre, which is LO-4.

Distance 12 and half-chord 5 give the radius 13 and hence the diameter 26. C-4.3-LO-4's bisection property with Pythagoras. (The answer field holds a section banner instead of a solution; see the defect list.)
Each parallel chord is bisected by the perpendicular from the centre, giving distances 4 and 3; on opposite sides these add. C-4.3-LO-4 applied twice.
The central angle theorem proved in full, by drawing the diameter through C and using the isosceles triangles. C-4.3-LO-5's first clause.

Justifies the supplementary opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral from the four isosceles triangles at the centre. C-4.3-LO-6's proof, by a route that does not go through the central angle theorem.
MN being a diameter gives a right angle at P (LO-5), and the cyclic quadrilateral's supplementary angles then relate the two angles asked about (LO-6). Both theorems are used in sequence.

Part (i) doubles 110 degrees to get the reflex angle at the centre (LO-5); part (ii) uses the supplementary opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral APQR (LO-6). Part (iii) then falls out of the isosceles triangle OPR.
OP perpendicular to BC bisects the chord, which is what makes CP equal to x (LO-4); the equilateral arrangement of three equally spaced seats about the centre is the circumcircle picture of LO-2.

Part (i) solves the supplementary opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral ABCD (LO-6); the pipe segments EF and GH are chords whose lengths and distances from the centre come from LO-4's bisection property.
The circle as the locus of points equidistant from a fixed point. C-4.3-LO-1's definition.
Defines centre, radius, chord, diameter and arc in one item -- the whole vocabulary list of C-4.3-LO-1.
Matches four of those terms to their descriptions. Same C-4.3-LO-1 vocabulary, tested by matching.
The longest chord is the diameter. A definitional relation between chord and diameter, C-4.3-LO-1.
Why the diameter/chord relation is one-way: a diameter must also pass through the centre. C-4.3-LO-1, asked as a justification.
True/false on the diameter being the longest chord. The same C-4.3-LO-1 fact as qid:706700.
Gap-fill naming a central chord the diameter. C-4.3-LO-1 vocabulary.
Radius is half the diameter. The numerical form of C-4.3-LO-1's radius/diameter relation.
Defines the radius, including that it is the same for every point of the circle. C-4.3-LO-1.
False: a radius joins the centre to the circle, while a chord joins two points OF the circle. A definitional boundary, C-4.3-LO-1.
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle -- the deduction C-4.3-LO-5 names explicitly.
Derives the right angle from the central angle theorem applied to a straight angle. Both clauses of C-4.3-LO-5 in one answer, which is why it is the code rather than a bare recall.
The assertion is the semicircle result and the reason is the 180 degree central angle that produces it. C-4.3-LO-5.
Gap-fill for the 90 degrees a diameter subtends on the circle. C-4.3-LO-5.
Three vertex positions on the same semicircular arc, all giving a right angle -- a drawn demonstration that the result is independent of the vertex, which is the force of C-4.3-LO-5.
Exactly one circle through three non-collinear points. C-4.3-LO-2, as a one-mark recall.
Argues from the two perpendicular bisectors meeting in one point, and from their being parallel when the points are collinear. C-4.3-LO-2's full reasoning, including the degenerate case.
The compass-and-straight-edge construction of the circumcircle, which is how C-4.3-LO-2 says the circumcentre is located.
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord -- C-4.3-LO-4's first clause, stated.
Chord 16 in a radius-10 circle gives a distance of 6, via the bisection property and Pythagoras. C-4.3-LO-4.
States and explains all three chord properties -- bisection, its converse, and equal chords being equidistant. C-4.3-LO-4 in full.
The 5-12-13 version of the same computation as qid:706716. C-4.3-LO-4.
The RHS congruence proof that the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. C-4.3-LO-4's 'proves that' clause.
Halves an 80 degree central angle to get the angle on the remaining circumference. C-4.3-LO-5's first clause, numerically.
True/false on the doubling relation between centre and circumference. C-4.3-LO-5.

The major-arc point gives half of 110 degrees (LO-5); the minor-arc point requires the reflex angle of 250 degrees, and the resulting 125 and 55 degrees are supplementary, which is the cyclic-quadrilateral relation of LO-6.
